doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Free playing needs technique and hearing; Bird's chord notes
summary: Free playing is no excuse for lacking technique or ear; Jordan describes how Bird used upper tones rather than spelling chords.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Before I leave this, there was two things I wanted to point out. One that your bass player said, he says if you had an improviser who didn’t really have a tone or a sound then this would fail. You have to be familiar with silence and all kinds of sounds to carry this out. He’s saying that to play this kind of music you’ve got to have some juice to your sound already. In other words you were talking about you’ve got to be able to play your instrument first. That just playing free is not an excuse for lack of technique.

Oh that’s right, that’s right exactly. And it’s not an excuse for not being able to hear. See that’s, when they first started in New York especially, everybody would be going on the stand and trying, twenty or fifteen people just running on and on and over. But when it boiled down and later on as the music kept developing all of those stopped coming on the stand. I mean it started getting to the point where people knew you got to hear in order to know what you’re doing, I don’t care how out it is. And there’s a lot of people still playing free that doesn’t — how can it say it — that doesn’t come in whatever the chord or whatever the sound is, you can hear that the sound is here and they’re somewhere else and never would get to the sound of the tune. And say like beboppers, sometimes there were beboppers like Charlie Parker. Everybody said Charlie Parker played changes. But Charlie Parker didn’t play changes like people play changes now like running up the chords or whatever. And that’s another thing, when I studied Bird and saw where Bird, when I finally learned how chords was when I was young and finally did Bird, he didn’t do any note in the chord. Play a C chord and Bird had an A, an F-sharp, a B-flat. You know all the tops. I didn’t know then, but Bird, I knew a C chord and he didn’t have a note in a C chord. So don’t tell me — you know that’s one of the things that kind of turned me off, I said Bird got some other kind of secrets. I said man you’re not playing the changes. Well it’s a C chord, they don’t have an A, before I know a sixth or whatever, he’d have an A, got an F-sharp, a G-sharp, got all kinds of things in it, you understand what I’m talking about. But now, when you hear people saying [scats] spelling out chords, you know, like the real Beboppers, they can play things I mean they can hook all that up and it sounds good, but it sounds like a mechanical kind of thing you know. Now that’s good, I don’t down nobody for doing it because I hear cats man just sit down and play like that and say wow, they can play “Cherokee” and “I Got Rhythm” and what’s another tune, and when I learned those tunes I said I went through that, but when I learned it I said this is good but I don’t want to say hey, you know, look at me as a poster child being able to play this because I got the rhythm because the rhythm was straight ahead notes. You know, straight across without anything, and with me I mean I don’t want to play that. I don’t want to play it. And then, the way I want to play I may jump from the low B-flat to the high F-sharp or D-flat over that, so that’s not going to work in going straight down chord patterns. You understand what I’m talking about? And that’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
